The Milwaukee Bucks are an American professional basketball team based in Milwaukee.
The Milwaukee Bucks compete in the National Basketball Association (NBA).
The Milwaukee Bucks play in the Central Division of the Eastern Conference.
The Milwaukee Bucks were founded as an expansion team in 1968.
Herb Kohl was the long-time owner of the Milwaukee Bucks until April 16, 2014.
On April 16, 2014, a group led by Wes Edens and Marc Lasry agreed to purchase a majority interest in the Milwaukee Bucks from Herb Kohl.
The sale of the Milwaukee Bucks was approved by the owners of the NBA and its Board of Governors on May 16, 2014.
Jon Horst manages the Milwaukee Bucks.
The Milwaukee Bucks have won two league championships (1971, 2021).
The Milwaukee Bucks have won three conference titles (Western: 1971, 1974; Eastern: 2021).
The Milwaukee Bucks have won 19 division titles (1971–1974, 1976, 1980–1986, 2001, 2019–2024).
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Giannis Antetokounmpo have been named the NBA's Most Valuable Player while playing for the Milwaukee Bucks.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Giannis Antetokounmpo are the only players to win Finals MVP for the Milwaukee Bucks franchise.
The Milwaukee Bucks are the only NBA team to have won a championship in both the Eastern and Western Conference.
The Milwaukee Bucks were awarded a franchise on January 22, 1968, by the NBA.
A fan contest was held to name the new Milwaukee Bucks team.
The most-voted fan entry for the team's nickname was the Robins.
The judges chose "Bucks" as the team's nickname, which is a reference to Wisconsin's official wild animal, the white-tailed deer.
R. D. Trebilcox argued that bucks were "spirited, good jumpers, fast and agile," leading to his award of a new car for reasoning why "Bucks" was a good nickname.
The Milwaukee Bucks returned to the NBA after 13 years in 1968.
The previous team based in Milwaukee, the Hawks, played four seasons in the early 1950s before moving to St. Louis in 1955 (now based in Atlanta).
The first season of the Milwaukee Bucks (1968–69) was a struggle.
The Milwaukee Bucks' first victory came on their sixth game against the Detroit Pistons, winning 134-118.
The Milwaukee Bucks won only 26 more games in their first year as an expansion team.
In the inaugural season of the Milwaukee Bucks (1968–69), they had a coin flip with the Phoenix Suns to see who would get the first pick in the upcoming draft.
The Milwaukee Bucks won the coin flip and secured the first pick, but had to win a bidding war with the New York Nets for Lew Alcindor of UCLA.
During his six seasons with the Milwaukee Bucks (1968–74), Kareem Abdul-Jabbar averaged 30.4 points and 15.3 rebounds per game.
The Milwaukee Bucks finished second-best in the league behind the New York Knicks during the 1969-70 season, with a record of 56-26.
The Milwaukee Bucks defeated the Philadelphia 76ers in five games in the Eastern Conference semifinals but were dispatched by the Knicks in five games in the Eastern finals.
Kareem Abdul-Jabbar was selected as the NBA Rookie of the Year for the 1969–70 season.
During his second season with the Milwaukee Bucks (1970), Oscar Robertson was traded to complement Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.
The Milwaukee Bucks finished the 1970-71 season with a record of 66-16, the second-most wins in NBA history at that time and still a franchise record.
During the regular season, the Milwaukee Bucks recorded a then-NBA record 20-game win streak during the 1970-71 season.
The Milwaukee Bucks won their first NBA championship on April 30, 1971, by sweeping the Baltimore Bullets in four games.
By winning the championship in only their third season, the Milwaukee Bucks became one of the fastest true expansion teams in North American professional sports history to win a league championship.
The Milwaukee Bucks remained a powerhouse for the first half of the 1970s.
In 1972, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar publicly announced his name change from Lew Alcindor to Kareem Abdul-Jabbar after privately converting to Islam.
The Milwaukee Bucks reached the division/conference finals for three consecutive years (1973-75) but lost in six games each time against the Los Angeles Lakers.
In 1973, the Milwaukee Bucks recorded their third consecutive 60-win season, becoming the first NBA team to do so.
Injuries resulted in an early playoff exit for the Milwaukee Bucks during the 1974-75 season.
The Milwaukee Bucks traded Kareem Abdul-Jabbar to the Los Angeles Lakers on June 16, 1975, for Elmore Smith, Junior Bridgeman, Brian Winters, and David Meyers.
After trading Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, the Milwaukee Bucks had several seasons in transition.
In 1976, Jim Fitzgerald and his partners sold the Milwaukee Bucks to Herb Kohl.
Don Nelson became head coach of the Milwaukee Bucks in November 1976 after Larry Costello resigned abruptly.
The Milwaukee Bucks drafted Kent Benson, Marques Johnson, and Ernie Grunfeld in the 1977 NBA draft.
Sidney Moncrief made his debut with the Milwaukee Bucks in 1979.
Don Nelson won two NBA Coach of the Year awards with the Milwaukee Bucks during seasons where they won division titles (1983 and 1985).
On October 18, 1977, Abdul-Jabbar punched Benson during a game, breaking his hand in the process.
Benson never played as aggressively again after the incident between Abdul-Jabbar and himself.
The Milwaukee Bucks traded Benson to the Detroit Pistons for Bob Lanier on December 30, 1980.
The Milwaukee Bucks won the Midwest Division title in 1980.
After losing to Seattle in the semi-finals, the Milwaukee Bucks moved to the Eastern Conference's Central Division.

During the 1979-80 season, the Milwaukee Bucks became perennial Eastern Conference contenders due to strong play from players like Sidney Moncrief, Marques Johnson, Paul Pressey, Junior Bridgeman, Craig Hodges, Terry Cummings, Ricky Pierce, and Jack Sikma.
The Milwaukee Bucks' colors were forest green, deep red, and white until 1978 when they added various shades of green to the uniforms.
In 1985, the Milwaukee Bucks eliminated red from their team colors.
The Milwaukee Bucks became the first NBA team to sweep the Boston Celtics in a best-of-seven playoff series during the 1983 season.
During the 1987 NBA playoffs, Julius Erving's final game was hosted by the Milwaukee Bucks.
In 1985, Herb Kohl bought the Milwaukee Bucks after fears that out-of-town investors could buy the team and move it out of Milwaukee.
Before the transaction was complete, Lloyd Pettit and his wife Jane Bradley Pettit announced they were donating a new arena called the Bradley Center.
In 2003, after considering selling the team, Herb Kohl decided against selling the Bucks to Michael Jordan and would continue owning them, improving them, and committing to remaining in Wisconsin.
On May 21, 2012, the naming rights of the Bradley Center were sold to BMO Harris Bank, a division of Bank of Montreal.
After the heirs to the Bradley fortune gave their approval, the arena was renamed the "BMO Harris Bradley Center."
For most of the 1990s, the Milwaukee Bucks franchise was mired in mediocrity under coaches Frank Hamblen, Mike Dunleavy, and Chris Ford.
The Milwaukee Bucks made the playoffs only three times during the 1990s (1992, 1995, 1998).
During the 1990s, the Milwaukee Bucks suffered a franchise-record seven straight losing seasons from 1991 through 1998.
The Milwaukee Bucks drafted Glenn Robinson with the first overall pick in the 1994 NBA Draft and acquired Ray Allen in a draft-day trade with the Minnesota Timberwolves in 1996.
In 1998, the Milwaukee Bucks selected Dirk Nowitzki with the ninth overall pick but traded him to the Dallas Mavericks for Robert Traylor.
The Milwaukee Bucks overhauled their logo and uniforms during their 25th anniversary in 1993.
The primary color scheme was altered when red was supplanted by purple.
Purple road uniforms replaced the former green away uniforms.
In 1997, the Milwaukee Bucks sent Vin Baker to the Seattle SuperSonics in a three-team trade and acquired Terrell Brandon and Tyrone Hill from the Cleveland Cavaliers.
They also traded Danny Fortson, Johnny Newman, and Joe Wolf to the Denver Nuggets for Ervin Johnson.
The Milwaukee Bucks finished their season with a 36-46 record during the 1997-98 season, failing to make the playoffs for the seventh consecutive time.

After reaching its zenith in 2000-2001 by winning 52 games and their first division title in 15 years, the Milwaukee Bucks reached the 2001 Eastern Conference Finals but lost to the Philadelphia 76ers in seven games.
The "Let It Fly" era became known for the high-scoring offense of the team, personified by Ray Allen and Tim Thomas.
In 2001, behind strong encouragement from George Karl, the Milwaukee Bucks acquired forward Anthony Mason at the beginning of the 2001-02 season.
However, Mason struggled with his weight and had a tough time finding his role in the team.

The Milwaukee Bucks went into a swoon during February and March of the 2001-02 season, culminating with a loss to the Detroit Pistons on the final night of the season, which eliminated them from the playoffs and gave the division to the Pistons.
The collapse created tension between George Karl and the players, resulting in a trade of Ray Allen to Atlanta for Toni Kukoč and a 2003 first-round draft pick (used to select T. J. Ford).
During the 2002-03 season, the Milwaukee Bucks traded Ray Allen and backup Ronald "Flip" Murray to the Seattle SuperSonics for Gary Payton and Desmond Mason.
The trade allowed Michael Redd to see increased playing time, and with Payton in the backcourt, they finished the season with a 42-40 record.
The Milwaukee Bucks made the playoffs but lost in the first round to the New Jersey Nets in six games during the 2002-03 season.
Sam Cassell and Ervin Johnson were traded to Minnesota for Joe Smith during that offseason.
Payton left via free agency after playing only 28 games for the Bucks.
Karl's tenure also ended after the 2002-03 season.
Within a one-year period, the team had lost both their coach and players most responsible for the team's success during that era.
Michael Redd played for the Milwaukee Bucks under Larry Harris as general manager from 2004 to 2010.
The Milwaukee Bucks struggled with inconsistency and injury for six years after Michael Redd's tenure, reaching the playoffs twice (2004, 2006).
During that period, they were defeated by the Detroit Pistons in five games each time.
Michael Redd blossomed into an all-star and a perimeter shooting threat during his time with the Bucks, becoming the new "face of the franchise."
The Milwaukee Bucks received the first pick in the 2005 NBA draft and used it to select center Andrew Bogut.
Andrew Bogut struggled with inconsistency and injuries in his first four years in Milwaukee but over time became a key contributor to the team.
In 2006, the Milwaukee Bucks finished last in their division (40-42) but still made the playoffs as an eighth seed against the Detroit Pistons.
They were eliminated by the Pistons in a 4-1 series loss during the first round of the playoffs.
The Milwaukee Bucks announced that they would not renew general manager Larry Harris's contract, which was to expire in June.
In April, John Hammond, formerly vice-president of basketball operations for the Pistons, was hired as the new general manager.
Scott Skiles, formerly of the Chicago Bulls and Phoenix Suns, became head coach after Larry Krystkowiak was relieved of his duties.
On June 26, 2008, the Milwaukee Bucks acquired Richard Jefferson from the New Jersey Nets in a trade for Yi Jianlian and Bobby Simmons.
Later that day, they selected West Virginia's Joe Alexander with the eighth pick of the NBA draft.
Alexander became the first Taiwanese-born player in the NBA.
In the 2009 NBA draft, the Milwaukee Bucks selected point guard Brandon Jennings who had not gone to college but played in Italy the previous year.
Midway through the season, Hakim Warrick was traded to the Chicago Bulls, and John Salmons joined the team.
Salmons averaged a team-leading 19.9 points per game during his time with the Bucks.
The play of Jennings, along with the improvement of Andrew Bogut, Ersan İlyasova, and the Salmons trade, made the Milwaukee Bucks a playoff contender.
In October, the Bucks clinched a playoff berth on April 6, 2010, by defeating the Chicago Bulls in a road win.
The "Fear the Deer" slogan started during that time and became the team's battle cry in the NBA playoffs.
The Bucks finished the regular season with a record of 46-36 and clinched the sixth seed but were eliminated in a seven-game series against the Atlanta Hawks.
In the 2010-11 season, the Milwaukee Bucks finished ninth in the Eastern Conference, just out of reach of the playoffs.
Bogut was sidelined for the rest of the season due to a broken arm after making an awkward fall during a dunk in a late-season game.
The Milwaukee Bucks traded both Bogut and Stephen Jackson to the Golden State Warriors on March 13, 2012, for Monta Ellis, Ekpe Udoh, and Kwame Brown.
Before the 2012 NBA draft, the Bucks sent Shaun Livingston, Jon Brockman, and Jon Leuer to the Houston Rockets in exchange for a first-round pick and Samuel Dalembert.
In the 2012 draft, the Bucks selected Doron Lamb and John Henson.
After 32 games of the 2012-13 season, Jim Boylan was fired as head coach after leading the team since 2008.
Larry Drew was announced as the interim head coach and led the Bucks to a 22-28 record to finish the season at 38-44.
The Milwaukee Bucks qualified as the eighth seed but were quickly swept by the Miami Heat in four games during the playoffs.
Jim Boylan was relieved of his coaching duties, and Larry Drew was hired as head coach.
On June 27, 2013, Giannis Antetokounmpo was selected with the 15th overall pick of the 2013 NBA draft by the Milwaukee Bucks.
They also brought in O. J. Mayo, Carlos Delfino, Zaza Pachulia, and Gary Neal as well as seeing Monta Ellis opt-out of his final year contract.
The Bucks agreed to sign-and-trade Brandon Jennings to the Detroit Pistons for Brandon Knight, Khris Middleton, and Viacheslav Kravtsov.
By the start of the 2013-14 season, only four players from the previous season's roster remained with the Milwaukee Bucks.
The 2013-14 season was a struggle for the Bucks as they finished with the worst record in the league at 15-67 and the worst record in team history.

On April 16, 2014, Herb Kohl agreed to sell a majority interest of the Milwaukee Bucks to New York-based billionaires Wes Edens and Marc Lasry for $550 million while retaining a significant minority interest.
The new owners were expected to keep the team in Milwaukee and contribute $100 million toward building a new arena for the franchise.
Approval from the NBA Board of Governors came on May 15, 2014, a month later.
By this time, Bradley Center was seen as obsolete.
The donation from the Bradley heirs did not provide for the arena's operating expenses or long-term capital needs.

This led the NBA to give an ultimatum to Edens and Lasry – unless the Bucks were either close to getting a new arena or actually opening one by the 2017-18 season, they would be required to return the franchise to the league, which would sell it to prospective ownership groups in Las Vegas and Seattle.

On July 1, 2014, Jason Kidd was secured as the coaching rights for the Milwaukee Bucks from the Brooklyn Nets in exchange for two second-round draft picks in the 2015 NBA draft and the 2019 NBA draft.
With the acquisition of Kidd, Larry Drew was fired as head coach.
The Milwaukee Bucks' new slogan for the 2014-15 season became "Own The Future."
The Bucks' overall play vastly improved during Jason Kidd's tenure.
On December 26, 2013, the Bucks beat the Atlanta Hawks 107-77 to match their win total of the previous season just 30 games in.
From January 24 to February 20, 2014, the Bucks went on a stretch where they won 10 out of 12 games (10-2).

On February 11, 2014, the Bucks beat the Sacramento Kings for their 30th win of the year and became the first-ever NBA team to double their win total from the previous season before the All-Star Break.
Larry Sanders was released after several off-court incidents that led to multiple suspensions.
On February 19, 2014, Brandon Knight was traded to the Phoenix Suns for Michael Carter-Williams, Miles Plumlee, and Tyler Ennis during the final minutes of the trade deadline.
Jabari Parker suffered a season-ending knee injury on December 15, 2013, in a game against the Phoenix Suns.
The NBA passed the 'Jay-Z Rule' on January 25, 2014, prohibiting ownership groups from consisting of more than 25 individuals and mandating that no ownership interest be smaller than 1%.
